concept.shortExplanation: Attention looks at every token simultaneously, which means that on its own it cannot tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'. Position has to be added to the input explicitly. The sinusoidal scheme gives every position a signature built from sine and cosine waves at geometrically spaced frequencies, so nearby positions are similar, distant ones are not, and the pattern extends to lengths never seen in training. The waves are pure mathematics; the token vectors they are added to are real embeddings.
concept.ahaMoment: Position is not a number the model looks up — it is a pattern mixed into the meaning vector itself. The same word at two positions is genuinely two different vectors by the time attention sees it.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The embedding model could not be downloaded, so encodings cannot be combined with real token vectors. Retry once you have a connection — it works offline afterwards.

levels.title: Read the Signature
levels.instructions: Each encoding stripe belongs to one position. Identify which. The values are computed from the sinusoidal formula at the dimensions shown.
hints: Compare the mystery stripe against the candidate rows highlighted in the reference heatmap below it — this is a matching task, not something to compute by hand.

Low dimensions (the left side of the stripe) oscillate fastest, so they're the most sensitive to small position changes. High dimensions on the right barely change between neighbouring positions, which is why nearby positions are so easy to confuse and distant ones aren't.
For this seed, the six rounds' real positions in order are 23, 5, 25, 26, 13, 15 — matched by comparing the fast-oscillating left dimensions first, since they disambiguate nearby candidates fastest.

levels.title: Keep Positions Distinct
levels.instructions: Set the model dimension and frequency base so that positions across the sequence stay distinguishable. Distinctness is one minus the average similarity between position vectors — nearby positions are meant to resemble each other, so the average is what matters, not the closest pair. More dimensions only help while the base is small enough to give them different frequencies.
hints: Push the base as low as it goes first, then raise the dimension count — a small base is what lets extra dimensions carry genuinely different frequencies instead of all crawling at nearly the same rate.

More dimensions isn't free: at base 100000, 128 dimensions actually scores worse than 4 (0.294 vs 0.509) because most of them oscillate too slowly to vary at all over 64 positions and just add redundant, near-identical columns. At base 10, 128 dimensions beats 4 by a wide margin (0.848 vs 0.610) because every one of them now carries a genuinely different frequency.

dModel = 64 with base = 10 (the range's own minimum) measures 0.8495 — just past the 3-star line. That's a real ceiling for this maxPosition, not an arbitrary round number: 128 dimensions at base 10 actually measures very slightly lower, 0.8480.

levels.title: Word Plus Position
levels.instructions: Real token embeddings, real encodings, added together as the transformer does it. Given two sentences that differ only in word order, predict how much the combined vectors diverge — then check against the measured value.
hints: All three real divergences are small — none reach even 0.09 — because only one word moves in each pair and cosine similarity is bounded. Guessing the same middling number for all three gets you close in aggregate but won't separate the pairs from each other.

The size of the divergence tracks how far the moved word travels, not the sentence's meaning: "only" shifting by a single slot changes much less than "dog"/"man" swapping across the whole clause. Raising the scale slider past ~1 barely moves any of the numbers further — the effect saturates quickly.

At the default scale (1): "the dog bit the man" vs "the man bit the dog" diverges about 0.086 (the biggest jump — a 3-position move); "only she told him that" vs "she told only him that" about 0.025 (the smallest — a 1-position move); "rain before sunset" vs "sunset before rain" about 0.047.
